title: THE VERSE MONEY CAN’T BUY: What Paul Really Meant When He Said “The Love of Money Is the Root of All Kinds of Evil”
paragraphs: THE VERSE MONEY CAN’T BUY: What Paul Really Meant When He Said “The Love of Money Is the Root of All Kinds of Evil”

Money may be sitting in your wallet without owning your heart. Or you may have almost nothing—and still be completely possessed by the desire for more. First Timothy 6:10 was never merely a warning for rich people. It was a warning about what the human heart can turn into a god.
There is a frightening possibility hiding behind one of the most misquoted verses in the Bible.
You can have money without worshiping money.
And you can worship money without having much of it.
That second sentence is the one we don't like.
Because it means the warning Paul gave Timothy cannot be safely handed to billionaires, celebrities, corrupt politicians, greedy executives, or somebody with a bigger house than ours.
It can find us in a rented room.
It can find us counting coins.
It can find us checking our bank balance at midnight.
It can find us staring at someone else's success and quietly wondering why God gave them what we desperately wanted.
It can find us working overtime.
Building a business.
Trying to feed our children.
Dreaming of escaping debt.
Wanting a better life.
None of those things automatically makes us greedy.

But somewhere between needing money and trusting money, between using money and serving money, between possessing something and being possessed by it, the human heart can cross a line almost invisibly.
And Jesus knows exactly where that line is.
You have probably heard someone say:
"Money is the root of all evil."
That is not what Scripture says.
Paul's actual warning is far more precise—and far more uncomfortable.
In 1 Timothy 6:10, the Greek text begins:
“ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία…”
Rhiza gar pantōn tōn kakōn estin hē philargyria…
The crucial word is φιλαργυρία — philargyria.
It is formed from words associated with affection or love and silver/money. Its sense is love of money, avarice, greed for wealth.
Paul is not identifying coins, currency, salaries, businesses, savings accounts, houses, or possessions as inherently evil.
He is exposing an affection.
A love.
A craving.
A heart that begins looking to wealth for what only God can ultimately provide.
And the sentence continues with devastating consequences:
“…ἧς τινες ὀρεγόμενοι ἀπεπλανήθησαν ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως…”
Some, Paul says, by reaching or craving after it, wandered away from the faith.
Then comes one of the darkest images in the passage: they pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
Notice who does the piercing.
This is not the picture of God gleefully destroying people for possessing money.
It is the picture of human beings pursuing something they believed would save them, only to discover that the thing they embraced had become a blade.
That changes the verse completely.
Money isn't presented as the Savior.
Money isn't presented as Satan.
Money is something the heart can turn into an idol.
And idols always overpromise.
Money whispers:
"When you finally have enough, you will be safe."
Jesus says:
“Do not be anxious about your life.”
Money whispers:
"When you finally have enough, people will respect you."
Jesus kneels and washes feet.
Money whispers:
"When you finally have enough, you will matter."
The cross says you mattered enough for Christ to shed His blood for sinners.
Money whispers:
"More."
Jesus says:
“Follow Me.”
And suddenly this isn't an article about somebody else's greed anymore.
It's about ours.
Maybe you've never considered yourself materialistic because you aren't wealthy.
But greed doesn't require a mansion.
Sometimes greed lives in envy.
Sometimes it hides beneath comparison.
Sometimes it sounds like:
"I'll finally be happy when I can afford that."
"I'll finally feel successful when people see what I've accomplished."
"I'll finally relax when there is enough in the account."
"I need what they have."
"I deserve more."
And sometimes the problem isn't even wanting luxury.
Sometimes fear itself begins making money feel like a functional savior.
That distinction matters because Scripture does not condemn responsible provision.

Paul writes elsewhere that people should provide for those entrusted to their care. Proverbs repeatedly commends wisdom, diligence, prudence, and preparation. Scripture contains faithful people who possessed significant resources and used what they had in ways connected to God's purposes.
The biblical answer to greed, therefore, is not financial irresponsibility.
It is reordered worship.
Read the verses immediately preceding Paul's famous warning and the context becomes unmistakable.
“But godliness with contentment is great gain.”
Then Paul reminds us of something every funeral eventually proves:
We brought nothing into this world.
We can carry nothing out.
Nothing.
The infant arrives without a bank account.
The billionaire leaves without his portfolio.
The king cannot put his kingdom into the coffin.
The laborer cannot carry his final paycheck across eternity.
Your house stays here.
Your clothes stay here.
Your investments stay here.
Your trophies stay here.
Even the phone in your hand eventually belongs to someone else, gets thrown away, or disappears into history.
And one day somebody else may stand inside the room you spent decades paying for.
That isn't meant to make life meaningless.
It is meant to expose what is eternal.
You were never created to build your identity around things you cannot keep.
Paul's argument becomes even clearer later in the same chapter.
He does not tell wealthy Christians simply to cease possessing anything.
Instead, in 1 Timothy 6:17, he tells Timothy to warn the rich not to become arrogant and not to set their hope on “the uncertainty of riches.”
Then Paul redirects their attention to God, who richly provides.
And what should people with resources do?
Do good.
Become rich in good works.
Be generous.
Be ready to share.
That is extraordinarily important.
If money itself were inherently evil, generosity would simply be the redistribution of evil.
But Scripture's concern is deeper.
Who owns whom?
Do you possess your possessions?
Or do your possessions possess you?
Can God interrupt your plans?
Can He ask you to give?
Can He tell you that enough is enough?
Can someone else's success make you rejoice instead of resent?
Can your identity survive financial loss?
Can your heart remain grateful when your neighbor has more?
Could you obey Jesus even if obedience cost you financially?
Those questions reveal things a bank statement never will.
And Jesus had already given an even sharper warning.
“No one can serve two masters.”
Then He named the rival.
God and mammon.
The issue is not merely having resources.
The issue is mastery.
Money makes a terrible master because it can never say, “Enough.”
There is always another level.
Another purchase.
Another upgrade.
Another zero.
Another comparison.
Another person ahead of you.
Another reason to worry that what you accumulated might disappear.
And that is one of greed's cruelest scandals.
It promises freedom while quietly creating slavery.
You thought you owned the money.
Then you discovered the money owned your peace.
You thought you owned the house.
Then the house owned your image.
You thought you owned the career.
Then the career owned your identity.
You thought you were building security.
Then one financial crisis revealed how much of your security had never been resting in Christ.
But this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come merely to make greedy people slightly more generous.
He came to give sinners new hearts.
The answer to the love of money isn't simply, “Try harder not to like money.”
The answer is discovering a Treasure infinitely greater.
Christ.
Jesus tells of a treasure hidden in a field, so valuable that the man joyfully sells everything to obtain that field.
Notice the word that changes everything:
joyfully.
When Christ becomes the Treasure, surrender stops looking merely like deprivation.
We begin discovering something better.
That is Christianity.
Not Jesus standing beside your idols begging for equal shelf space.
Jesus becoming so precious that idols begin losing their shine.
And no one embodied that better than Christ Himself.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 8:9 that though Christ was rich, for our sake He became poor, so that through His poverty we might become rich.
This is not a promise that every Christian will become financially wealthy.
The riches of the Gospel are infinitely greater than that.
The eternal Son humbled Himself.
The King entered our poverty.
The sinless Christ took the place of sinners.
The One through whom all things were made entered a world obsessed with possessions, status, power, and self-preservation—and walked willingly toward a cross.
Judas sold Jesus for silver.
Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
Think about that contrast.
Human greed asked:
“What will you give me?”
Divine love said:
“I give Myself.”
At Calvary, the deepest poverty of humanity was exposed.
Our problem was never that we didn't have enough money.
Our problem was that we were separated from God by sin and utterly incapable of purchasing our redemption.
You cannot buy forgiveness.
You cannot finance justification.
You cannot purchase adoption into God's family.
You cannot bribe death.
You cannot negotiate your way into resurrection.
You cannot swipe a card at the gates of heaven.
Redemption required a price no human bank account could touch.
Peter says we were not redeemed with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
There it is.
The Gospel destroys both pride and despair.
The poor person cannot say, “God cannot love me because I have nothing.”
The wealthy person cannot say, “God must accept me because I have everything.”
Both stand at the same cross.
Both need the same blood.
Both need the same grace.
Both need the same Savior.
Maybe money has been controlling you.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you have compromised your integrity to make more.
Maybe generosity feels painful because every possession has wrapped another thread around your heart.
Maybe debt came through decisions you are ashamed to admit.
Maybe envy has poisoned friendships.
Maybe you secretly resent God because somebody else prospered while you struggled.
Maybe you've been chasing success because somewhere deep inside, you wanted finally to feel important.
Maybe you've even used ministry, business, or “blessing” language to disguise ambition that stopped being about Christ a long time ago.
Bring it into the light.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Repentance does not mean pretending money doesn't matter.
Rent matters.
Food matters.
Education matters.
Medical bills matter.
Providing for family matters.
Wise stewardship matters.
But none of those things requires money to become your god.
Repentance says:
“Jesus, this belongs to You too.”
My income.
My ambitions.
My fear.
My debt.
My possessions.
My business.
My plans.
My future.
My definition of success.
Everything.
Because Christianity is not inviting Jesus into one compartment of your life while Mammon holds the keys to another.
Christ is Lord.
And perhaps the most beautiful evidence that money is losing its throne is not poverty but freedom.
Freedom to give.
Freedom to share.
Freedom to say no to excess.
Freedom to enjoy God's provision without worshiping it.
Freedom to succeed without becoming arrogant.
Freedom to struggle without believing God abandoned you.
Freedom to hold possessions with open hands.
Freedom to say:
“If God gives, I will thank Him. If God asks me to give, I will obey Him. If circumstances strip away what I cannot keep, Christ will still be my Treasure.”
That is wealth the market cannot measure.
So don't walk away from this article merely saying, “Money isn't evil.”
That would miss Paul's warning almost entirely.
Ask the harder question:
What does my heart love?
Because the danger was never merely what was inside your wallet.
It was what might be sitting on the throne.
If someone immediately came to your mind while reading this, don't use the article as a weapon against them.
Love them.
Pray for them.
Then share it with them.
There may come a day when the promotion arrives, the business succeeds, the money starts flowing, and you need these words more than you do today.
Or there may come a day when everything becomes painfully tight and you need to remember that an empty account does not mean you have an empty Savior.
It doesn't.
Only Jesus saves.
Grace cannot be bought.
Your support can become part of sending truth farther.
Share Christ.
Share Scripture.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done for you.

Because somewhere tonight, somebody is exhausting their soul chasing the next paycheck, the next promotion, the next possession, the next symbol of success—hoping that if they can just obtain enough, the emptiness will finally become quiet.
They need to know there is another Treasure.
His name is Jesus.
Money can buy a bed but cannot guarantee rest.
It can purchase medicine but cannot purchase resurrection.
It can buy security systems but cannot conquer death.
It can purchase entertainment but cannot manufacture lasting joy.
It can buy influence but cannot purchase innocence.
It can pay debts between people.
But it cannot pay the debt of sin.
Only Christ could do that.
And He did.
So earn honestly.
Provide faithfully.
Save wisely.
Give generously.
Enjoy God's gifts gratefully.
Help the poor.
Support Gospel work as God enables you.
But never kneel before what was created to remain in your hand.
Money is a tool.
Christ is Lord.
And if money has already become more than a tool—if greed, envy, fear, status, or the hunger for more has dragged your heart somewhere you never intended to go—the story does not have to end there.
Peter denied Jesus.
The thief came to the cross with nothing.
Zacchaeus had allowed money to deform his life, yet an encounter with Jesus produced repentance and radically changed what he did with his possessions.
Grace rewrites people.
Jesus still calls sinners home.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still breaks idols.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still transforms hearts that finally stop defending themselves and surrender.
So come back.
Not when you've fixed everything.
Not when your finances look respectable.
Not when you've finally become generous enough to impress God.
Come to Christ empty-handed.
That's how every one of us comes.
And remember this when the world tells you your value is measured by what you can accumulate:
The greatest Treasure you will ever possess is the One who chose to give Himself to possess you.
